read.sections.0.heading.source: Start with what you can see

read.sections.0.text.note: 'Bố cục' for composition (glossary); 'quan sát' for observation per KEY_TERMS, used as a noun ('những quan sát'). In Vietnamese 'quan sát' is mostly a verb; a reviewer may want 'nhận xét' or 'điều quan sát được'. | Review: Same blue/green fix. [Reviewer changed: một dòng sông xanh → một dòng sông xanh dương]
read.sections.0.text.source: When you look at an artwork, begin with what you can see. Name the colours, people, objects and any words. Notice the composition, which means how the parts are arranged. In the poster, a blue river runs through the centre. Three people carry buckets towards one tap, and a child points at a cracked pipe. These are observations. They are facts that anyone can check by looking. The words “Water for every street” are also part of the evidence. Only after you look closely should you decide what the artwork might mean.
read.sections.0.text.back: When you look at a work of art, start with what you see. Name the colours, people, objects and any words. Notice the composition, meaning the way the parts are arranged. On the poster, a green river flows through the very middle. Three people carry buckets towards a tap, and a child points at a cracked pipe. These are observations. They are things anyone can check by looking. The words "Water for every street" are also part of the evidence. Only after looking carefully should you decide what the work might mean.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Art has told stories for a very long time
read.sections.1.heading.back: Art has been telling stories for a very long time

read.sections.1.text.note: Real places: Algeria (kept in Latin form; Vietnamese also writes 'An-giê-ri'), Tassili n'Ajjer (kept), Sahara, Trung Quốc, Vanuatu, Thái Bình Dương. 'Hà mã' hippos; 'bò' for cattle (the English says herds of cattle). 'Thanh minh thượng hà đồ' is the usual Vietnamese (Sino-Vietnamese) name of the Qingming scroll; check. 'Những người vẽ trên cát' for 'sand drawers'; 'một đường dài liền nét' for one continuous line. 'Cuộn tranh' for painted scroll (glossary). | Review: Vietnamese says the Vanuatu line is 'liền nét' (unbroken); English only says 'one long line' (accurate per UNESCO but slightly added). Scroll title kept as the usual Vietnamese name 'Thanh minh thượng hà đồ' while the English is 'Along the River During the Qingming Festival'; native speaker to confirm.
read.sections.1.text.source: People around the world use art to tell stories and keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock art shows hippos and herds of cattle. The land there is desert today, so the pictures tell us the Sahara was once much greener. In China, there is a painted scroll more than five metres long. It shows over 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. It is called Along the River During the Qingming Festival. In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long line. Their drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.
read.sections.1.text.back: People all over the world use art to tell stories and keep knowledge. At Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria, rock paintings show hippos and herds of cattle. Today that land is desert, so the paintings tell us the Sahara was once much greener. In China there is a scroll painting more than five metres long. It shows more than 800 people shopping, travelling and working in a busy city about 900 years ago. It is called Qingming Shanghe Tu (Thanh minh thượng hà đồ). In Vanuatu, in the Pacific, sand drawers use one finger to draw one long unbroken line. The drawings help people remember stories and knowledge.

read.sections.1.simpler.note: 'Các con vật sống gần sông' simplifies 'hippos'; check it does not change the meaning (the check question uses hippos and cattle).
read.sections.1.simpler.source: People all over the world tell stories with art. In Algeria, old rock art shows cows and river animals. Now the land is desert. So the art tells us the land was once green. In China, a long painted scroll shows a busy city. It shows more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw in the sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: People all over the world tell stories with art. In Algeria, ancient rock paintings show cattle and animals living near rivers. Now that land is desert. So the paintings tell us this place was once green. In China, a long scroll painting shows a busy city. It shows more than 800 people. They shop, work and travel. In Vanuatu, people draw in the sand with one finger. The drawings help them remember stories.

read.sections.2.text.note: 'Cách diễn giải' for interpretation (alternative 'diễn giải', 'cách hiểu'). 'Đối tượng' for audience is ambiguous (it also means 'object' or 'target'); alternatives 'khán giả', 'công chúng', 'người xem'. A reviewer must decide. 'Có thể' and 'có lẽ' for 'may' and 'might'.
read.sections.2.text.source: An interpretation is an idea about what an artwork means. A strong interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks the poster is about people who do not have enough water. The line of people at one tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe, because the child points right at it. Both ideas use evidence, so both can make sense. It also helps to think about the audience, the people the artist wanted to reach. Words like “may” and “might” show that you are being careful.
read.sections.2.text.back: An interpretation is an idea about what a work of art means. A convincing interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks the poster is about people who do not have enough water. The line of people at a tap and the words at the bottom support this idea. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe, because the child points straight at it. Both ideas use evidence, so both make sense. It is also good to think about the audience, meaning the people the artist wants to reach. Words like "might" and "perhaps" show that you are being careful.

read.sections.2.simpler.note: Check 'đối tượng' is clear with the explanation 'Nghệ sĩ muốn tiếp cận ai?'.
read.sections.2.simpler.source: An interpretation is an idea about what art means. A good one points to details. Viewer 1 thinks some people do not have enough water. Many people wait at one tap. That is a clue. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. The child points at it. Both ideas use evidence. Think about the audience too. Who did the artist want to reach? Use words like “may” and “might”.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: An interpretation is an idea about the meaning of art. A good interpretation points to details. Viewer 1 thinks some people do not have enough water. Many people stand waiting at a tap. That is a clue. Viewer 2 thinks the poster asks the town to fix the pipe. The child points at it. Both ideas use evidence. Think about the audience too. Who does the artist want to reach? Use words like "might" and "perhaps".

watch.summary.note: 'Bảo tàng Ayala' for Ayala Museum; 'salakot' kept (a Philippine hat); 'mũ đan rộng vành' describes it. 'Chiếc bình nhỏ màu xanh lá từ Trung Quốc có hai con rồng' - check against the Lesson 15 translation of the same video. | Review: Must match Lesson 15's Vietnamese description of the same video (jar, salakot, cloth); check consistency.
watch.summary.source: This is the same short video from Lesson 15. It comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, watch closely for details. The video shows a small green pot from China with two dragons on it. It shows a salakot, a wide woven hat, decorated with shell and silver. It also shows a small cloth with a poem sewn into it. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the pot unusual, because most pots like it were plain. The shell and silver suggest that an important person owned the hat. The poem tells us how the cloth's owner felt. A careful viewer first says what they see. Then they say what it might mean, and which details support that idea.
watch.summary.back: This is a short video like the one in Lesson 15. The video comes from the Ayala Museum in the Philippines. This time, look closely at the details. The video shows a small green jar from China with two dragons on it. It shows a salakot, a wide-brimmed woven hat, decorated with shell and silver. It also shows a small piece of cloth with a poem embroidered on it. Each detail is a clue. The dragons make the jar unusual, because most jars like it are plain. The shell and silver suggest that an important person once owned the hat. The poem tells us the feelings of the owner of the cloth. A careful viewer first says what they see. Then they say what it might mean, and which details support that idea.
